analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal child labor to employ anyone under 18 handling tobacco plants or dried leaves.
analysis.headline: The bill to bar children under 18 from handling tobacco was introduced with 32 cosponsors in June 2021 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act, the main federal wage-and-hour law, to treat the employment of anyone under 18 who touches tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves as "oppressive child labor" — the same category of work the law flatly prohibits. It was introduced in June 2021 with 32 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee. The committee never held a hearing or voted, and no chamber ever considered the bill before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Child and teenage farmworkers gain the most: the bill would take 16- and 17-year-olds out of direct contact with tobacco, which is absorbed through the skin and linked to nicotine poisoning, and would end an exemption that lets agriculture escape the hazardous-work standards applied to other industries. Their families and rural communities benefit indirectly from safer work.

how_it_helps.text: It amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so that employing anyone under 18 in direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves counts as 'oppressive child labor,' a category of child labor the law prohibits outright.

It removes tobacco farming from the agricultural exemption in the child labor law, closing a loophole that has let children under 18 legally work around tobacco even though federal rules bar them from similarly hazardous jobs in manufacturing and mining.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco growers and leaf-buying companies would bear the cost: losing access to under-18 labor means paying adult workers and may raise the price of domestically grown leaf. Some farming families would also lose income their teenagers currently earn.

drawbacks.text: The bill would end a longstanding, legal source of work for teenagers in tobacco-growing regions; 16- and 17-year-olds who currently earn wages in tobacco fields would lose that employment outright, not gain protections.

The ban is categorical: it draws no line between 12- and 17-year-olds or between light and heavy tasks, so critics could argue it sweeps in work that older teens perform without injury, raising compliance questions for small family farms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—removing children under 18 from direct contact with a known health hazard and a demanding physical job—comes at essentially no cost to the general public, and the affected employers are a small number of tobacco farms. The strongest objection is that teenage farm work is a legal and, in many farming communities, traditional way to earn money, and a hard age-18 cutoff would also bar 16- and 17-year-olds from work some families want. On the merits, the health case for the bill outweighs that cost, which is why its death in committee without any hearing or vote is hard to defend on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and nothing ever happened to it there—no hearing, no vote, no floor action—so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 14, 2021 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
No further action was taken after that referral: the record shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate companion activity before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill's final status on Congress.gov is that it died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco growers and leaf buyers keep the legal ability to employ minors in direct contact with tobacco, a labor source and cost structure that would have changed under the bill. Child workers in tobacco fields gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House on June 14, 2021.

for.name: 32 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Bass, Norton, McGovern, Schakowsky, Blumenauer, Grijalva, Chu, and Velazquez.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Bobby Scott, D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican sponsored the bill; because it never reached the floor, there was no roll-call to show how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill would make it illegal to employ anyone under 18 in direct contact with tobacco plants or dried leaves, cutting off a workforce some tobacco farms have relied on. Growers would have to shift to adult labor, which generally costs more.

Companies that purchase American-grown leaf sit atop a supply chain that child welfare groups have repeatedly documented as employing minors; a legal prohibition on child contact with tobacco would raise their compliance burden and costs. Their interest in keeping leaf cheap runs against child workers' protection.
